prompt: In Spark's default mode, what happens to a sale between reaching the topic and being counted?

choices.text: It waits for the next micro-batch
choices.why: Right. Spark gathers what arrived since the last batch and processes the slice together.

choices.text: Spark counts it the moment it arrives, like a consumer's poll loop
choices.why: That is the wrong picture the section starts from: by default Spark works in slices.

choices.text: It waits for the night, when Spark rereads the whole table
choices.why: Spark never reruns the query over the whole table; it is incremental.

choices.text: It is copied to a file and read by a batch job
choices.why: Nothing is copied to a file first; the batch reads the topic directly.

prompt: Which of these queries needs Spark to keep state between micro-batches?

choices.text: Keep only the sales from Natal
choices.why: A filter: one row in, at most one row out, nothing to remember.

choices.text: Turn the value's bytes into text
choices.why: A projection needs nothing from earlier batches.

choices.text: Total cents per shop per hour
choices.why: Right. The running totals of open windows are carried from batch to batch.

choices.text: Drop the `book` column
choices.why: Picking columns is stateless.

prompt: A search turns up Spark code built on `DStream` objects. What does the section say about it?

choices.text: It is the older API, deprecated, with no notion of event time
choices.why: Right. Structured Streaming, the one with `readStream`, replaced it.

choices.text: It is Structured Streaming's low-level layer, used for windows
choices.why: Windows are written with DataFrame functions; DStreams are the old API.

choices.text: It is the continuous-processing API from section 07
choices.why: Continuous processing is a trigger of Structured Streaming, not DStreams.

choices.text: It is the Python name for what Scala calls a DataFrame
choices.why: The two APIs are different, not two spellings of one.

prompt: What does `pip install pyspark==4.1.3` put on the machine?

choices.text: Only a Python client that talks to a Spark server installed separately from the Apache site
choices.why: No separate install: the package carries Spark's Java libraries itself.

choices.text: Spark itself, Java libraries included
choices.why: Right. It starts Spark inside your program when a session is asked for.

choices.text: Spark and a copy of Java 21 for it to run on
choices.why: Java comes from lesson 1's apt-get; the package uses it.

choices.text: Spark and its Kafka connector
choices.why: The connector is not in the package; it is fetched on first use.

prompt: A colleague's program asks for `spark-sql-kafka-0-10_2.12:3.5.1` while running pyspark 4.1.3. What does the section lead you to expect?

choices.text: It works, because the connector only talks to Kafka
choices.why: The connector runs inside Spark and must match its Scala and Spark versions.

choices.text: Ivy refuses to download it
choices.why: The download succeeds; the trouble starts when Spark loads it.

choices.text: A Java error about a missing class or method at the first read
choices.why: Right. Both numbers disagree with the installed Spark, and the error does not name versions.

choices.text: A warning, after which Spark picks the right version itself
choices.why: Spark loads what it was given; nothing corrects the coordinates.

prompt: In the checkpoint directory, a batch that has a file in `offsets` and none in ___ is a batch that did not finish.
What type does Spark give the `value` column of a Kafka topic?

choices.text: binary
choices.why: Right. The sale is bytes until the query casts and parses it.

choices.text: a struct with the sale's fields
choices.why: Spark does not know the value is JSON; `from_json` makes the struct later.

choices.text: string
choices.why: It has to be cast to a string; that is what `cast` is for.

choices.text: map of text to text
choices.why: There is no parsing at all before your query does it.

prompt: Why would a five-minute window over Spark's `timestamp` column count the sales wrongly here?

choices.text: It is in UTC and the shops are three hours behind
choices.why: The session time zone is set; the problem is which moment it records.

choices.text: It is when the record was sent
choices.why: Right. The sale's moment is `at`, inside the value.

choices.text: It is the time Spark read the record
choices.why: It is Kafka's record timestamp, set when the record was produced.

choices.text: It is empty unless the broker sets it
choices.why: It was filled; it showed today's date.

prompt: Why does the lesson run its Spark programs with `2>spark.log`?

choices.text: Spark refuses to start when its messages go to a terminal
choices.why: It starts either way; this is about what you read.

choices.text: So that the checkpoint is written to the file
choices.why: The checkpoint is a directory of its own.

choices.text: Spark's chatter goes to a file you read when something fails
choices.why: Right. The screen keeps what the query printed; errors are still in the file.

choices.text: It hides errors, which are harmless in a lab
choices.why: The errors are kept, in the file, and the lesson reads them there.

prompt: Put the steps of `spark_sales.py`'s query in the order the program applies them.
items: Declare a watermark of two minutes on at
Write the stream with an output mode

prompt: Match each output mode to what it prints after a batch.

pairs.right: the windows that batch changed, totals so far
windows the watermark has closed, once each

right_distractors: windows that got no sale in that batch

prompt: In the append run, the latest sale seen by the end of batch 0 was at 09:10:12 and the watermark delay is two minutes. At what minute past nine does the watermark used by batch 1 fall? (Answer in whole minutes.)
The append run never printed the 09:30 window. A colleague concludes those sales were lost. What is the better reading?

choices.text: They were late, and Spark dropped them behind the watermark
choices.why: Nothing was late; the window is waiting, not dropped.

choices.text: Append mode prints only the first six windows of any query
choices.why: There is no such limit; what decides is the watermark.

choices.text: It waits in state for the watermark
choices.why: Right. It stopped at 09:34:41, and a later sale would release it.

choices.text: Partition 2 held them, and Spark never read it
choices.why: Partition 2 is empty; the sales are counted in state.

prompt: Batch 0 of the update run showed a 09:10 window with one sale before the 09:05 window was complete. Why?

choices.text: The till's clock went backwards
choices.why: The till's clock only moves forward; the order broke across partitions.

choices.text: Ten records of partition 0 reached further into the morning than forty of partition 1
choices.why: Right. Order holds inside a partition, not across them.

choices.text: Spark sorts the rows of every batch by shop before counting, which moves Caruaru's sales first
choices.why: No sort happens; the batch took a slice of each partition.

choices.text: Update mode prints the windows of each batch in reverse order, newest first, before older ones
choices.why: Order of printing is not the issue; the window really had one sale so far.

prompt: Why is complete mode a poor fit for counts per five-minute window on a stream that runs for months?

choices.text: It prints nothing until the stream ends
choices.why: It prints after every batch; the problem is how much it keeps.

choices.text: It refuses a watermark
choices.why: It accepts one and does not use it to drop windows.

choices.text: Its state never shrinks
choices.why: Right. It suits a result that stays small, like a total per shop.

choices.text: It double-counts a window each time it is printed
choices.why: Each print repeats the total; it does not add to it.

prompt: Where does a Spark streaming query keep the offsets it has read?

choices.text: In its checkpoint directory
choices.why: Right. Not in Kafka, which is why the group list was empty.

choices.text: In a consumer group's commits on the broker
choices.why: Spark assigns itself partitions and never commits; `--list` showed nothing.

choices.text: In `spark.log`
choices.why: That file is only where the lesson sends Spark's messages.

choices.text: In memory, until the program ends
choices.why: A restart found them, so they are on disk.

prompt: The second run with the same checkpoint printed nothing, although the query says `startingOffsets` is `earliest`. Why?

choices.text: The topic's retention had deleted the old sales
choices.why: The sales were still there; the checkpoint said they were done.

choices.text: `earliest` only applies to a query's first run
choices.why: Right. After that the checkpoint decides where to start.

choices.text: Console output is shown once per checkpoint
choices.why: Batch 6 printed later with the same checkpoint.

choices.text: Spark had crashed during the first run
choices.why: The first run finished; its commits were written.

prompt: The process dies after `offsets/9` is written and before `commits/9`. What does the restart do?

choices.text: Skips batch 9 and plans batch 10 from the latest offsets
choices.why: Skipping would lose the records batch 9 was going to read.

choices.text: Starts again from the topic's earliest offset
choices.why: The checkpoint keeps it from going back that far.

choices.text: Asks Kafka for the group's last committed offset
choices.why: There is no group; the position lives in the checkpoint.

choices.text: Runs batch 9 again with the same offsets
choices.why: Right. The sink may then receive batch 9 twice.

prompt: After the restart, the sale from Natal at 09:21 appeared in no output. What happened to it?

choices.text: It went to partition 2, which Spark ignores
choices.why: Spark reads every partition; the reason is its time.

choices.text: It fell behind the watermark
choices.why: Right. Its window had been forgotten, and a late sale is dropped silently.

choices.text: It was added to the 09:35 window
choices.why: The 09:35 window grew by the Recife sale only: 13 to 14.

choices.text: The producer rejected it as malformed
choices.why: Both lines were sent; only one changed a window.

prompt: Which triggers end by themselves once the data present at the start has been read? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: availableNow
choices.why: Yes: several batches, respecting limits, then it stops.

choices.text: once
choices.why: Yes: one batch, then it stops; it is deprecated in favour of availableNow.

choices.text: processingTime of five seconds
choices.why: It keeps starting batches every five seconds until stopped.

choices.text: continuous
choices.why: It never ends; the interval is how often progress is saved.

prompt: Why did the continuous trigger refuse `spark_sales.py` before reading a record?

choices.text: Continuous processing cannot read from Kafka
choices.why: Kafka is one of the sources it supports.

choices.text: The checkpoint directory already existed from an earlier run of the query
choices.why: It was a new directory; the message named the watermark.

choices.text: The query keeps state, which continuous mode does not support
choices.why: Right. It takes row-in, row-out queries only; the watermark was the first objection.

choices.text: Python cannot ask for that trigger
choices.why: Python asked for it; Spark analysed the query and refused.

prompt: While the live query ran, roughly how many megabytes did the Spark process and the Kafka node hold together? (Answer to the nearest 100.)
The file sink refused update mode. Why does it accept only append?

choices.text: A written file is never changed, so only final rows can go in
choices.why: Right. Update would need to rewrite rows already on disk.

choices.text: JSON cannot hold numbers that change
choices.why: The format is not the issue; changing a file already written is.

choices.text: Update mode needs Kafka's keys
choices.why: The console sink takes update mode with no keys at all.

choices.text: Append is faster on disk
choices.why: Speed is not why; correctness is.

prompt: A batch to the Kafka sink is replayed after a crash, and `09:05` with 28 sales is written twice. Which downstream reader is hurt?

choices.text: One that keeps the last value per key
choices.why: The second copy replaces the first with the same number: no harm.

choices.text: A compacted topic's reader
choices.why: Compaction keeps the last per key, which is still 28.

choices.text: Spark itself, on its next batch
choices.why: Spark does not read its own output back from Kafka.

choices.text: One that adds each record to a running total
choices.why: Right. Each record is a whole count, not an increment, and adding it twice doubles it.

prompt: What lets the file sink ignore files left by a batch that crashed half-written?

choices.text: Kafka's transactions
choices.why: The file sink does not use Kafka to write.

choices.text: The `_spark_metadata` log naming each finished batch's files
choices.why: Right. Files no entry names are not part of the output.

choices.text: The random part of each file's name, which changes when a batch runs again
choices.why: The random name avoids collisions; it does not say which files count.

choices.text: Empty files mark failed batches
choices.why: Empty files are normal: a shuffle partition with no rows.

prompt: Ponto Final wants a stock count per book, updated in a database table every few seconds, with no total counted twice after a crash. Which combination fits this lesson?

choices.text: Complete mode to the console, with the query restarted every night after closing
choices.why: The console keeps nothing, and the database never sees the counts.

choices.text: Continuous trigger to a file sink
choices.why: Continuous refuses state, and files refuse update mode.

choices.text: Update mode, a checkpoint, and an upsert in foreachBatch
choices.why: Right. A replayed batch overwrites the same rows and can be recognised by its id.

choices.text: Append mode with no watermark, so that every row goes out as soon as it arrives
choices.why: Append needs a watermark to know when a result is final.

prompt: A teammate deletes `~/spark/ckpt/update` to tidy up, then runs the update query again on the same topic. What do they see?

choices.text: Nothing, as in the second run
choices.why: That nothing came from the checkpoint, which is gone.

choices.text: Only the sales added since the last run
choices.why: Without a checkpoint Spark has no idea what the last run read.

choices.text: The whole topic counted again from batch 0
choices.why: Right. `earliest` applies again, as for a new query, and the old state is gone.

choices.text: An error, because the query's id is missing
choices.why: A missing directory is a new query, not an error.
